Chapter 7. Guiding Children Toward Personal Ownership of Faith.
As children step into adolescence and young adulthood, something shifts. Their questions get deeper, and their need for independence starts to shine through. If you’re a parent, you’ve probably felt this tug—wanting to guide, but not control. It’s a natural, even necessary, part of growing up. The trick? Supporting their journey, while letting them find their own path.
Picture teaching your child to ride a bike. At first, you’re right there, steadying the seat—offering encouragement, maybe a reassuring word or two. But as they wobble forward, you slowly let go, trusting they’ll find their balance, even if it means a few shaky starts and the occasional tumble.
Helping kids take real ownership of their faith is a lot like that. It’s about encouraging honest exploration. Let them ask tough questions, express doubts, try new experiences, and look for answers in ways that make sense to them.
Instead of just handing out answers, offer resources—maybe a thoughtful book, a podcast, or connecting them with someone who can speak to their interests and questions.
And here’s something to pay attention to: Respect their pace. Some kids grab hold of faith quickly, while others need more time and space. Both are completely okay.
Affirm their unique journey. Remind them faith isn’t a competition or a checklist. It’s about a personal relationship that unfolds over time, in its own way.
Imagine your teenager wants to check out a different church service, join a youth group, or get involved in a service project. They might even head in a direction that’s unfamiliar to your family. These moments are golden opportunities—show interest, ask thoughtful questions, and support their choices, even if they don’t exactly match what you’ve always known.
And sometimes, kids might step away from faith for a while. Honestly, that can be tough to watch. But often, it’s just part of them making their beliefs truly their own. The best things you can do? Keep the conversation open, offer unconditional love, and trust in the seeds you’ve already planted.
So, what’s the real goal here? Not to create mini versions of your own faith, but to empower your kids to build something authentic and resilient. When you do that, you’re helping them walk into adulthood ready to face life’s complexities—with confidence and integrity.
